title: Medicaid and Mortality: New Evidence from Linked Survey and Administrative Data
research_question: Does expanding public health insurance eligibility to low-income near-elderly adults reduce their mortality? How large are the effects on overall mortality and on deaths from disease-related versus external causes, and how do these effects evolve over time following coverage gains?
data_description: The study links three data sources at the individual level. The 2008–2013 American Community Survey (restricted-use, ~50% larger than public version) provides socioeconomic characteristics including family income, educational attainment, citizenship, and SSI receipt. These records are linked via Census Protected Identification Keys to (1) the Census Numident file, which provides date of death through 2017 from Social Security Administration records, and (2) Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services administrative Medicaid enrollment records (2008–2016). Cause-of-death information comes from the Mortality Disparities in American Communities project, which links the 2008 ACS to National Death Index records (2008–2015). The primary analytic sample comprises approximately 566,000 U.S. citizens aged 55–64 in 2014 with family income below 138% of the federal poverty line or less than a high school degree, excluding SSI recipients. The unit of observation is the individual-year, with annual mortality as the main outcome.
institutional_context: The Affordable Care Act sought to expand Medicaid eligibility nationwide to all adults in families with incomes below 138% of the federal poverty line, beginning in 2014. Previously, Medicaid generally covered only pregnant women, individuals with disabilities, and very low-income parents. A 2012 Supreme Court decision made the expansion optional for states. As a result, 21 states implemented the expansion in January 2014 (with Michigan in April 2014), while additional states expanded in 2015 (NH, PA, IN), 2016 (AK, MT), and 2017 (LA); other states declined to expand. Approximately 13.6 million adults gained Medicaid coverage under the ACA. The ACA also required states to permit hospital presumptive eligibility determinations and federal law mandated retroactive coverage for up to three months prior to application. This staggered, partial state adoption created variation in exposure to expanded public coverage among otherwise similar low-income near-elderly adults across states.
